{{distinguish|Jensen's inequality}}
{{short description|Mathematical theory}}
In the mathematical [[theory of probability]], '''Janson's inequality''' is a collection of related inequalities giving an exponential bound on the probability of many related events happening simultaneously by their pairwise dependence. Informally Janson's inequality involves taking a sample of many independent random [[binary data|binary variables]], and a set of subsets of those variables and bounding the probability that the sample will contain any of those subsets by their pairwise correlation.

==Statement==

Let <math>\Gamma</math> be our set of variables. We intend to sample these variables according to probabilities <math>p = (p_i \in [0, 1]: i \in \Gamma)</math>. Let <math>\Gamma_p \subseteq \Gamma</math> be the random variable of the subset of <math>\Gamma</math> that includes <math>i \in \Gamma</math> with probability <math>p_i</math>. That is, independently, for every <math>i \in \Gamma: \Pr[i \in \Gamma_p]= p_i</math>.

Let <math>S</math> be a family of subsets of <math>\Gamma</math>. We want to bound the probability that any <math>A \in S</math> is a subset of <math>\Gamma_p</math>. We will bound it using the expectation of the number of <math>A \in S</math> such that <math>A \subseteq \Gamma_p</math>, which we call <math>\lambda</math>, and a term from the pairwise probability of being in <math>\Gamma_p</math>, which we call <math>\Delta</math>.

For <math>A \in S</math>, let <math>I_A</math> be the random variable that is one if <math>A \subseteq \Gamma_p</math> and zero otherwise. Let <math>X</math> be the random variables of the number of sets in <math>S</math> that are inside <math>\Gamma_p</math>: <math>X = \sum_{A \in S} I_A</math>. Then we define the following variables:

: <math>\lambda = \operatorname E \left[\sum_{A \in S} I_A\right] = \operatorname E[X]</math>

: <math>\Delta = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{A \neq B, A \cap B \neq \emptyset} \operatorname E[I_A I_B]</math>

: <math>\bar{\Delta} = \lambda + 2\Delta</math>

Then the Janson inequality is:

: <math>\Pr[X = 0] = \Pr[\forall A \in S: A \not \subset \Gamma_p] \leq e^{-\lambda + \Delta} </math>

and

: <math>\Pr[X = 0] = \Pr[\forall A \in S: A \not \subset \Gamma_p] \leq e^{-\frac{\lambda^2}{\bar{\Delta}}} </math>

===Tail bound===

[[Svante Janson|Janson]] later extended this result to give a tail bound on the probability of only a few sets being subsets. Let <math>0 \leq t \leq \lambda</math> give the distance from the expected number of subsets. Let <math>\varphi(x) = (1 + x) \ln(1 + x) - x</math>. Then we have

: <math>\Pr(X \leq \lambda - t) \leq e^{-\varphi(-t/\lambda)\lambda^2/\bar{\Delta}} \leq e^{-t^2/\left(2\bar{\Delta}\right)}</math>

== Uses ==

Janson's Inequality has been used in [[pseudorandomness]] for bounds on [[AC0|constant-depth]] circuits.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Limaye |first1=Nutan |last2=Sreenivasaiah |first2=Karteek |last3=Srinivasan |first3=Srikanth |last4=Tripathi |first4=Utkarsh |last5=Venkitesh |first5=S.  |title=Proceedings of the 51st Annual ACM SIGACT Symposium on Theory of Computing |chapter=A fixed-depth size-hierarchy theorem for AC<sup>0</sup>&#91;⊕&#93; via the coin problem |date=2019 | pages=442–453 |arxiv=1809.04092 |doi=10.1145/3313276.3316339 |isbn=978-1-4503-6705-9 |s2cid=195259318 }}</ref> Research leading to these inequalities were originally motivated by estimating [[Graph coloring#Chromatic number|chromatic numbers]] of [[random graph]]s.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Ruciński |first1=Andrzej |title=Janson inequality |url=http://www.encyclopediaofmath.org/index.php?title=Janson_inequality&oldid=16002 |website=Encyclopedia of Mathematics |accessdate=5 March 2020}}</ref>
